*Written by Claude (AI) with David Reinstein, 17 November 2026. Every number on this page is read from [`five-drivers-2026-11-17.json`](five-drivers-2026-11-17.json), which `scripts/five-drivers.mjs` computes from the current model (1,000,000 simulated worlds). Not yet reviewed by engineers or cell-culture experts.*

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fd = FileAttachment("five-drivers-2026-11-17.json").json()
money = v => v >= 100 ? `$${Math.round(v).toLocaleString("en-US")}` : v >= 10 ? `$${v.toFixed(0)}` : v >= 1 ? `$${(Math.round(v * 100 + 1e-6) / 100).toFixed(2)}` : `$${v.toFixed(v < 0.01 ? 3 : 2)}`
share = v => v === 0 ? "none" : v < 0.01 ? `${(100 * v).toFixed(2)}%` : `${(100 * v).toFixed(0)}%`
oneIn = v => `about 1 in ${(Math.round(1 / v / 100) * 100).toLocaleString("en-US")}`
A = fd.summary.all
C = fd.summary.under36
H = fd.summary.under100
R = fd.spread_removed_when_held_at_median
cellStyle = "padding:5px 8px;border-bottom:1px solid #e3e3e3;text-align:right;white-space:nowrap"
headStyle = "padding:5px 8px;border-bottom:2px solid #bbb;text-align:right;vertical-align:bottom;line-height:1.25"
```

## In brief

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<ul>
<li>The model works out what it would cost to produce one kilogram of cultured chicken cells (weighed dry) in a large, well-run plant using the technology of 2036. It does this ${fd.n.toLocaleString("en-US")} times, each time with a different combination of plausible inputs. Each run is one "simulated world".</li>
<li>Although the model has about thirty inputs, the cost comes down to <strong>five numbers</strong>, and three of them (all about the liquid the cells grow in) account for nearly all of the uncertainty.</li>
<li>In a typical simulated world the cells cost about ${money(fd.total.p50)} per kg dry. Chicken sells wholesale for about $3.50 per kg. Cultured cells would have to cost about $12 to $18 per kg dry to match that, and no simulated world gets there. Only ${oneIn(fd.price_lines[2].share_of_worlds_below)} gets under $36 per kg dry, roughly the price level of organic chicken.</li>
<li><strong>Running the plant and paying for it set a floor.</strong> Even if medium and growth factors were free, a kg of dry cells would cost about ${money(fd.floor.p50)} in a typical world, and only ${share(fd.floor.share_of_worlds_below["36"])} of worlds would come in under $36.</li>
<li>The arithmetic has been checked carefully. Most of the input ranges have not: many are placeholders without a source. So the model is best read as "what would have to be true for cultured meat to be cheap", not as a forecast.</li>
</ul>`
```

## 1. The cost is five numbers

The cost of a kilogram of dry cells is:

> **litres of medium per kg × (price of medium per litre + growth-factor cost per litre) + plant running costs + capital charge**

"Medium" is the nutrient liquid the cells grow in. "Growth factors" are signalling proteins added to the medium in tiny amounts; today they are very expensive. "Plant running costs" are labour, maintenance, energy, consumables and a few other proteins. The "capital charge" is the yearly cost of paying for the plant, spread over each kg it makes.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const rows = [
    ["Litres of medium per kg of dry cells", "litres", v => `${Math.round(v)} L`],
    ["Price of medium, per litre", "medium_price", money],
    ["Growth-factor cost, per litre of medium", "gf_per_litre", money],
    ["Plant running costs, per kg of dry cells", "running", money],
    ["Capital charge, per kg of dry cells", "capital", money]
  ];
  return html`<div style="overflow-x:auto"><table style="border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-size:0.95em">
  <thead><tr>
    <th style="${headStyle};text-align:left">The five numbers</th>
    <th style="${headStyle}">Typical world<br><span style="font-weight:400">(all ${fd.n.toLocaleString("en-US")})</span></th>
    <th style="${headStyle}">Worlds where cells cost under $100<br><span style="font-weight:400">(${share(H.share_of_worlds)} of worlds)</span></th>
    <th style="${headStyle}">Worlds where cells cost under $36<br><span style="font-weight:400">(${share(C.share_of_worlds)} of worlds)</span></th>
  </tr></thead>
  <tbody>
  ${rows.map(([label, key, f]) => html`<tr><td style="${cellStyle};text-align:left;white-space:normal">${label}</td><td style="${cellStyle}">${f(A.drivers[key])}</td><td style="${cellStyle}">${f(H.drivers[key])}</td><td style="${cellStyle}">${f(C.drivers[key])}</td></tr>`)}
  <tr><td style="${cellStyle};text-align:left;font-weight:600">Total cost per kg of dry cells</td><td style="${cellStyle};font-weight:600">${money(A.total_median)}</td><td style="${cellStyle};font-weight:600">${money(H.total_median)}</td><td style="${cellStyle};font-weight:600">${money(C.total_median)}</td></tr>
  </tbody></table></div>
  <p style="font-size:0.9em;color:#555">Each cell is the middle value (median) across the worlds in that column, so the rows do not multiply and add up exactly to the total.</p>`;
}
```

**How to read it.**

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<ul>
<li>In a typical world, a kg of dry cells takes about ${Math.round(A.drivers.litres)} litres of medium at about ${money(A.drivers.medium_price)} a litre. Medium is by far the largest cost: about ${money(A.lines_median.medium)} of the ${money(A.total_median)} total.</li>
<li>To get under $36 per kg, everything has to be low at once: about ${Math.round(C.drivers.litres)} litres of medium at about ${money(C.drivers.medium_price)} a litre (about ${money(C.lines_median.medium)} of medium per kg), almost no growth-factor cost, plant running costs of about ${money(C.lines_median.running)} and a capital charge of about ${money(C.lines_median.capital)}.${C.lines_median.running > C.lines_median.medium ? " In those worlds, running the plant costs more than the medium." : ""}</li>
<li>For comparison with published work: Pasitka and colleagues (2024) priced their medium at $0.63 a litre (stated in the paper's abstract). Alex Bates's <a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yjP2WTf3bWa_OjaTolOXJXydQDxH4ZsbcXMPOdrz2mo/edit">literature review</a> reports that their 20-day test run in a 1.8-litre vessel used about 64 litres of medium per kg of wet cells. That would be roughly 210 to 320 litres per kg of dry cells, depending on how much water the cells are assumed to hold, which is close to the model's typical world (${Math.round(A.drivers.litres)} litres). We could not confirm the 64-litre figure ourselves, because the paper's main text is behind a paywall. The paper's design for a full-size plant assumes much less medium: about 22 litres per kg of wet cells, or roughly 75 to 110 litres per kg dry (our calculation from its supplementary tables: $14.11 of nutrients per kg of wet cells at $0.63 a litre). Even that is well above the ${Math.round(C.drivers.litres)} litres of the worlds under $36.</li>
</ul>`
```

### Which of the five matters most?

One way to ask this: if we knew one of the five numbers for certain, how much of the spread in the model's cost would disappear?

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const order = Object.entries(R).sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);
  const pctOf = v => v < 0.005 ? "less than 1%" : `${Math.round(100 * v)}%`;
  return html`<div style="max-width:560px">${order.map(([k, v]) => html`<div style="display:grid;grid-template-columns:minmax(0,1fr) 6.5em;gap:8px;align-items:center;margin:4px 0">
    <div><div style="font-size:0.93em">${fd.drivers[k].label}</div><div style="height:9px;background:#e9eef3;border-radius:3px"><div style="height:9px;width:${Math.max(1, 100 * v)}%;background:#2a78d6;border-radius:3px"></div></div></div>
    <div style="text-align:right;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">${pctOf(v)}</div></div>`)}</div>
  <p style="font-size:0.9em;color:#555">Share of the spread in cost that disappears when that one number is held at its typical value. The shares do not add to 100%, because the numbers multiply as well as add.</p>`;
}
```

So nearly all of the model's uncertainty is about medium: how much of it a kg of cells needs, what a litre costs, and what the growth factors in it cost. Running costs and capital hardly affect the spread across all worlds. They matter in a different way.

::: {.callout-important}
## Running costs and capital are a floor

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p>Suppose medium and growth factors cost nothing at all. A kg of dry cells would still cost what it takes to run the plant and to pay for it: about ${money(fd.floor.p50)} in a typical world.</p>
<ul>
<li>Only ${share(fd.floor.share_of_worlds_below["36"])} of worlds would be under $36 per kg, ${share(fd.floor.share_of_worlds_below["18"])} under $18, and ${share(fd.floor.share_of_worlds_below["12"])} under $12.</li>
<li>In the worlds that do get under $36, running costs and capital together are about ${money(fd.floor.under36.floor_median)} of the ${money(fd.floor.under36.total_median)} total${fd.floor.under36.floor_median > fd.floor.under36.total_median / 2 ? ": more than half" : ""}.</li>
</ul>
<p>So cheap medium is necessary but not enough. Matching chicken would also need a plant that is much cheaper to build and run than the model's typical one. These two numbers have the weakest sourcing in the model (see section 4), which makes them a priority for expert input.</p>`
```
:::

## 2. What lies behind the five numbers

The five numbers are where the cost is added up. They are not the root causes. Each one depends on which technical developments succeed, and those developments are what research and investment could actually change.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const B = fd.behind, pc = v => `${Math.round(100 * v)}%`;
  const rows = [
    ["Litres of medium per kg", html`Mostly <strong>which production process works at scale</strong>, because the process sets how densely cells can be grown. The process used accounts for about ${pc(B.litres.process_used)} of the spread in this number. Typical medium use is ${Math.round(fd.by_process.fedbatch.litres_median)} litres with fed-batch, ${Math.round(fd.by_process.perfusion.litres_median)} with perfusion and ${Math.round(fd.by_process.continuous.litres_median)} with continuous culture. Nutrient yield (how many cells a litre of medium can feed) sets a lower limit, which applies in ${pc(B.litres.nutrient_floor_sets_medium_use_in_share_of_worlds)} of worlds.`],
    ["Price of medium per litre", html`Partly <strong>whether cheap plant-based "hydrolysate" medium can be used</strong> (about ${pc(B.medium_price.hydrolysates_usable)} of the spread): about ${money(B.medium_price.median_if_usable)} a litre if it can, ${money(B.medium_price.median_if_not)} if it cannot. The rest is the price range assumed within each case.`],
    ["Growth-factor cost per litre", html`Mostly <strong>whether cheap growth factors exist by 2036</strong> (about ${pc(B.gf_per_litre.cheap_growth_factors_exist)} of the spread): about ${money(B.gf_per_litre.median_if_cheap)} a litre if they do, ${money(B.gf_per_litre.median_if_not)} if they do not.`],
    ["Plant running costs", html`Entered directly as ranges for fixed costs, utilities and consumables, and added proteins. The model has <strong>no development behind them</strong>, and the ranges have no published source.`],
    ["Capital charge", html`Reactor price, how much reactor volume the plant needs (set by cell density and how fast the cells grow, so again by the process), plant size, the cost of borrowing and plant lifetime.`]
  ];
  return html`<div style="overflow-x:auto"><table style="border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-size:0.95em">
  <thead><tr><th style="${headStyle};text-align:left">The number</th><th style="${headStyle};text-align:left">What mainly decides it in the model</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>${rows.map(([a, b]) => html`<tr><td style="${cellStyle};text-align:left;white-space:normal;vertical-align:top;min-width:9em">${a}</td><td style="${cellStyle};text-align:left;white-space:normal">${b}</td></tr>`)}</tbody></table></div>
  <p style="font-size:0.9em;color:#555">"Share of the spread" means how much of the variation in that number, across simulated worlds, goes with that one factor taken alone.</p>`;
}
```

So the developments that matter are few: **a dense production process (perfusion or continuous culture) that works at commercial scale, cheap medium, cheap growth factors, and a plant that is cheap to build and run.** The model represents the first three thinly, as yes-or-no switches with a probability each plus a price range, and the fourth not at all.

<details><summary><strong>How much the process matters on its own</strong></summary>

"almost none" : share(P[k].share_under36)}</td></tr>`)}</tbody></table>
  <p style="font-size:0.9em;color:#555">Each row runs the model with that process only. In the default model a world uses fed-batch, perfusion or continuous culture with probabilities of ${Math.round(100 * P.fedbatch.share_of_worlds)}%, ${Math.round(100 * P.perfusion.share_of_worlds)}% and ${Math.round(100 * P.continuous.share_of_worlds)}%. The model does not yet charge perfusion and continuous culture for the extra equipment they need, so their advantage here is overstated.</p>`;

## 3. Reading the price lines

The pages quote costs in three ways, which is a common source of confusion:

- **Per kg of dry cells.** This is what the model calculates. Cells are mostly water, so a kg of dry cells is several kg of meat.
- **Per kg of meat made only of cells,** at the water content of chicken meat. This is the dry-cell cost multiplied by 0.275.
- **Per kg of a "hybrid" product:** cells mixed with plant-based ingredients costing \$3 a kg. This is how products are likely to be sold, and it is what the threshold cards on the main model page use.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The hybrid figures assume 25% cells. That is a convention, not a finding.
There is no agreed share of cells in a hybrid product. These pages use 25% as the baseline. Products on sale may contain less: in November 2026 UPSIDE Foods described the cell share of its new blended chicken only as "double-digit", meaning at least 10% ([Green Queen](https://www.greenqueen.com.hk/upside-foods-lab-grown-cultivated-chicken-launch-us-clearance/)). The fewer cells a product contains, the less the cost of the cells matters. The table below therefore shows a 10% version alongside the 25% baseline. You can change the share on the [Advanced model](index.qmd) under *Hybrid product*.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div style="overflow-x:auto"><table style="border-collapse:collapse;width:100%;font-size:0.95em">
<thead><tr>
  <th style="${headStyle};text-align:left">Price line</th>
  <th style="${headStyle}">Per kg of dry cells</th>
  <th style="${headStyle}">Per kg of meat made only of cells</th>
  <th style="${headStyle}">Per kg of hybrid product<br><span style="font-weight:400">(25% cells, the baseline)</span></th>
  <th style="${headStyle}">Per kg of hybrid product<br><span style="font-weight:400">(10% cells)</span></th>
  <th style="${headStyle}">Share of simulated worlds below it</th>
</tr></thead>
<tbody>${fd.price_lines.map(l => html`<tr>
  <td style="${cellStyle};text-align:left;white-space:normal">${l.label}</td>
  <td style="${cellStyle}">${money(l.dry)}</td><td style="${cellStyle}">${money(l.all_cell_meat)}</td><td style="${cellStyle}">${money(l.hybrid)}</td><td style="${cellStyle}">${money(l.hybrid_low_share)}</td>
  <td style="${cellStyle}">${share(l.share_of_worlds_below)}</td></tr>`)}</tbody></table></div>`
```

Two things follow from this table.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<ol>
<li><strong>The threshold cards on the main page are not parity lines.</strong> Wholesale chicken costs about $3.50 per kg. A hybrid product at $10 per kg is nearly three times that. So "about ${share(fd.price_lines[4].share_of_worlds_below)} of worlds are under $10 per kg of hybrid product" and "almost no worlds are price-competitive with chicken" are both true. They refer to different lines.</li>
<li><strong>A hybrid product hides most of the cell cost.</strong> With 25% cells, three quarters of it is cheap filler, so cells at $36 per kg dry give a hybrid at ${money(fd.price_lines[2].hybrid)} per kg. With 10% cells the same cells give ${money(fd.price_lines[2].hybrid_low_share)}, and even the model's typical world gives ${money(fd.price_lines[6].hybrid_low_share)}. That is why hybrid figures look so much closer to chicken than cell figures do, and why a product with few cells can be sold at a price near premium chicken while its cells remain expensive.</li>
</ol>`
```

## 4. How far to trust it

**What has been checked.** The arithmetic. The model has automated tests, and Alex Bates independently rebuilt it in November 2026; with the same settings his version reproduces ours exactly, world for world. His rebuild also found two logic errors, which were corrected on 17 November 2026 ([what changed](index.qmd)).

**What has not.** Most of the input ranges. Several of the inputs that matter most have no published source:

- plant running costs (the largest cost in the cheapest worlds);
- the probabilities that hydrolysate medium, cheap growth factors and food-grade proteins work by 2036 (75%, 50% and 70%);
- the favourable ends of the ranges for nutrient yield and medium price, which Alex's literature review finds more optimistic than the published evidence supports;
- how strongly good outcomes are assumed to arrive together (the "maturity" factor, explained in the [technical reference](docs.qmd#maturity-factor)).

**What that means.** The share of worlds that come out cheap depends mostly on how far those favourable ends reach and on whether they happen together. Neither has been asked of experts yet. Treat the model as a way to see what would have to go right, and how much, rather than as a prediction. The next step is to ask experts about the five numbers directly, and about the handful of breakthroughs behind them.

## 5. What this can and cannot tell a funder

**What it can tell you.**

- **How far away cheap cultured meat is, and what has to go right together.** For example, cheap medium alone is not enough (section 1), and plants using fed-batch almost never get near chicken prices (section 2). Work that cannot lead to a dense process, cheap medium and a cheap plant together does not lead to price parity.
- **Which unknowns are worth resolving first.** The numbers that carry most of the uncertainty, and those with the weakest sources, are where better evidence or expert judgement would change the answer most.
- **Whether a claim is consistent.** A company's stated price, cell share and scale can be checked against each other.

**What it cannot tell you.**

- **How much a research dollar changes the odds.** The model takes the probability that, say, hydrolysate medium works as an input. It contains nothing about how that probability responds to funding. So on its own it cannot say whether to fund cultured-meat research, or which line of research.
- **Cause and effect.** "Worlds where cells cost under \$36" are combinations of inputs that happen to come out cheap. They show what cheap cultured meat would look like, not how to bring it about.

**What would be needed to get from here to a funding decision.** First, judgements from experts about how much specific research or investment would shift the probabilities and ranges ("with this programme, and without it"). The model can then turn those shifts into a change in cost. Second, a view of how a lower cost changes how much cultured meat is sold and how much conventional meat it displaces; the [cost and demand page](demand.qmd) is a start on that.

## A possible shorter list of questions for experts {#shorter-questions}

*This is a draft for discussion. It has not been adopted, and it does not replace the questions the project already asks. It is here so that the team and the experts can react to it.*

The current plan asks experts about many of the model's individual inputs. Because the cost comes down to five numbers, one possibility is to ask about those five directly, and then about the few developments behind them. That would be about eight questions.

<details><summary><strong>Read the draft questions</strong></summary>

Each question is about a large plant built with the best technology available in 2036, and about cost in today's dollars. For each of the first five, we would ask for two values: your best single estimate, and a favourable value that you think has only about a 1-in-20 chance of being beaten.

**The five numbers**

1. **Medium needed.** How many litres of fresh medium would it take to produce one kg of cells (dry weight)?
2. **Medium price.** What would that medium cost per litre, leaving out growth factors and other added proteins?
3. **Growth factors.** What would growth factors cost per kg of cells (dry weight)?
4. **Running the plant.** What would it cost to run the plant per kg of cells (dry weight): labour, maintenance, energy, consumables and added proteins, leaving out medium, growth factors and the cost of building the plant?
5. **Building the plant.** How much would it cost to build the plant, per kg of cells (dry weight) it can produce each year?

**What would have to happen**

6. How likely is each of these by 2036: (a) food-grade medium that costs a small fraction of today's, by any route; (b) growth factors that are cheap, or cell lines that need very little of them; (c) perfusion or continuous culture working reliably at commercial scale?
7. If the first of these happens, how likely are the other two? (This tells us whether good outcomes tend to arrive together, which the model currently has to guess.)
8. Which single development would most change your answers to questions 1 to 5, and by roughly how much?

**What this would gain and lose.** Experts would answer fewer questions, in units closer to what they see in practice, and the answers would bear directly on the numbers that decide the cost. The detailed inputs would still be in the model, but they would be set to agree with the answers rather than asked about one by one. What would be lost is the detail on why a number is high or low; question 8 is there to recover some of that. Whether experts find these five numbers natural to estimate is itself something to test before relying on them.

</details>

## Terms used on these pages

<details><summary><strong>Open the list</strong></summary>

- **Simulated world** (also called a "draw"): one run of the model with one value chosen for every input.
- **Dry cell mass:** the weight of the cells with the water removed. Sources often quote costs per kg of *wet* cells, which are 70–80% water, so a wet figure is roughly a fifth to a third of the dry figure.
- **Nutrient yield:** grams of dry cells that one litre of medium can feed. It sets the least medium a kg of cells can use.
- **Medium-use multiplier:** how many reactor-fulls of fresh medium are used per reactor-full of cells harvested.
- **Hydrolysate:** a cheap digest of plant or yeast protein that could replace the purified amino acids in medium.
- **Hybrid product:** a product that is part cultured cells and part plant-based ingredients. These pages assume one quarter cells.
- **Maturity:** one number per simulated world that makes several technologies slightly more or less likely to work together. Its effect is small.
- **Price-competitive zone:** on Alex Bates's page, cells costing between \$12 and \$36 per kg dry, that is, between matching ordinary chicken and matching organic chicken.
- **Minimal set:** on Alex's page, one of the smallest combinations of things going well that gets a simulated world into the price-competitive zone.

</details>
